nodes.label: Muhammad dies
nodes.full: Muhammad dies at Medina without naming an unambiguous successor, leaving the community's leadership an open question the moment his authority disappears.

nodes.label: Byzantium & Persia exhaust each other
nodes.full: The 602-628 Byzantine-Sasanian war left both empires financially and militarily spent just before the Arab conquests began — a precondition the folio's own conquest entries take for granted rather than state outright.
nodes.src: background; Howard-Johnston, "Witnesses to a World Crisis" (2010)

nodes.label: Abu Bakr and the Ridda
nodes.full: Chosen at the Saqifa gathering over the Prophet's family's claims, Abu Bakr spent his two years holding Arabia together: the tribes that had followed Muhammad now refused Abu Bakr, and the 'wars of apostasy' reconquered the peninsula before the armies turned outward. He nominated Umar to succeed him.

nodes.label: Umar — the conquest state
nodes.full: Umar built the machinery a conquering movement needed: the stipend register (diwan) scaled by precedence in Islam, the garrison cities, the dating of documents from the Hijra, and the title 'Commander of the Faithful'. Syria, Egypt and Iraq were all taken under him. He was stabbed at prayer by a Persian captive in 644.

nodes.label: Uthman — the recension and the revolt
nodes.full: Uthman fixed the text of the Quran and staffed the provinces with his Umayyad kin. Grievances over the appointments, the treatment of dissidents and the control of conquered land converged on Medina, where rebels from Egypt and Iraq besieged his house and killed him — the first caliph murdered by Muslims.

nodes.label: Ali — the First Fitna
nodes.full: Ali moved the caliphate to Kufa and fought three wars: against Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr at the Camel; against Muawiya at Siffin, which ended in an arbitration; and against the Kharijites, who broke from him over that arbitration and killed him at prayer in 661.

nodes.label: Muawiya I makes the caliphate a dynasty
nodes.full: Muawiya had governed Syria for twenty years and had a standing army and a treasury. Ruling from Damascus on the Byzantine administrative model, he restored order after the fitna, then had his son Yazid recognised as heir — the step his critics never forgave.

nodes.label: Yazid I, Karbala and the Second Fitna
nodes.full: Yazid's accession was met by Husayn's march on Kufa, which ended in the massacre at Karbala (680), and by the revolt of Medina, crushed with a sack of the city at al-Harra (683). His army then besieged Mecca, where the Kaaba burned. Yazid and his son Muawiya II died within months, and the Sufyanid line ended.

nodes.label: Marwan I and the Zubayrid war
nodes.full: With the Sufyanids gone, Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr was acknowledged caliph across most of the empire from Mecca. The Syrian tribes chose Marwan, who won the Battle of Marj Rahit (684). His son then had to reconquer Iraq — from al-Mukhtar's pro-Alid Kufan regime and from the Zubayrids — before the empire was whole again.

nodes.label: Abd al-Malik refounds the state
nodes.full: After al-Hajjaj's siege killed Ibn al-Zubayr at Mecca in 692, Abd al-Malik rebuilt: an Arabic-language bureaucracy, a reformed aniconic gold and silver coinage, the Dome of the Rock, and al-Hajjaj installed as viceroy of the whole east.

nodes.label: Al-Walid I — the conquests at their limit
nodes.full: Under al-Walid, three fronts advanced at once: Tariq ibn Ziyad destroyed the Visigothic kingdom of Spain (711), Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Sind (711), and Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered the Sogdian cities of Transoxiana. Al-Walid also built the Great Mosque of Damascus.

nodes.label: Sulayman, Umar II and Yazid II
nodes.full: Sulayman staked everything on the second siege of Constantinople (717-718) and lost. His successor Umar II, the one Umayyad his enemies praised, tried to fix the tax injustice done to non-Arab converts and to end the ritual cursing of Ali. His early death and the reaction under Yazid II left the problem unsolved.

nodes.label: Hisham — the long holding operation
nodes.full: Hisham governed for nineteen years from a steppe palace, squeezing revenue, stalling the frontiers and putting down revolt after revolt — Zayd ibn Ali's rising in Kufa (740), the Kharijites, and the great Berber revolt that broke Umayyad North Africa. Historians call his reign the end of the 'jihad state'.
nodes.src: Blankinship, "The End of the Jihad State" (1994)

nodes.label: The Third Fitna and the fall of the Umayyads
nodes.full: Al-Walid II was murdered by his own family in 744, and the Syrian army destroyed itself in a Qays-Yaman civil war under three caliphs in two years. Marwan II moved the capital to Harran and held on until Abu Muslim's Khurasani army beat him at the Zab in 750 and hunted him down in Egypt.
nodes.src: al-Tabari; Sharon, "Black Banners from the East" (1983)

nodes.label: The wars of apostasy
nodes.full: On the Prophet's death much of Arabia repudiated Medina's authority, some following rival prophets — Musaylima in Yamama, Tulayha, the prophetess Sajah. Khalid ibn al-Walid's campaigns, above all the bloody Battle of Yamama, reconquered the peninsula in a year.
nodes.src: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri, via Sayf ibn Umar

nodes.label: Ajnadayn and Yarmuk — Byzantine Syria falls
nodes.full: Two battles broke Byzantine Syria: Ajnadayn in 634 and, decisively, the six-day fight on the Yarmuk in 636, where a Byzantine field army was destroyed against the river gorges. Heraclius withdrew behind the Taurus.
nodes.src: Kaegi, "Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests" (1992)

nodes.label: al-Qadisiyya, Jalula and Nihawand — the end of Sasanian Persia
nodes.full: Al-Hira surrendered on the road; al-Qadisiyya (636) opened Ctesiphon and the Sawad; Jalula and then Nihawand (642), 'the Victory of Victories', broke the last imperial army. The Persian court fled east until Yazdegerd III was murdered near Merv in 651.
nodes.src: al-Tabari, via Sayf ibn Umar; Pourshariati (2008)

nodes.label: The conquest of Egypt
nodes.full: Amr ibn al-As took Egypt with a small force against little Byzantine resistance: the fortress of Babylon fell in 641, Alexandria was surrendered by treaty in 642, and the garrison town of Fustat was founded beside the Nile.
nodes.src: "Chronicle of John of Nikiu"; al-Baladhuri; Aphrodito papyri

nodes.label: The Battle of the Camel and Siffin
nodes.full: The first war among Muslims: Ali defeated Aisha, Talha and al-Zubayr outside Basra in a battle named for the camel Aisha rode, then fought Muawiya to a standstill at Siffin. The agreement to submit the dispute to arbitrators split Ali's own army and created the Kharijites.

nodes.label: Karbala
nodes.full: Invited to Kufa and then abandoned by it, Husayn ibn Ali was surrounded by an Umayyad force on the desert plain of Karbala, cut off from the Euphrates, and killed with his male kin and companions. The day, Ashura, became the central rite of Shia Islam.

nodes.label: al-Harra, the Kaaba fire, and al-Mukhtar
nodes.full: The revolt of Medina ended in 683 with a three-day sack (al-Harra); the Umayyad siege of Mecca that followed left the Kaaba burned by fire from a catapult. In Kufa, al-Mukhtar seized the city in 685 in the name of a son of Ali, and was killed in 687 by the Zubayrids.

nodes.label: The first siege of Constantinople
nodes.full: Muawiya's fleets wintered at Cyzicus on the Marmara and pressed the capital for several seasons. The Byzantine account credits the invention of 'Greek fire' with breaking the campaign. The Arabs withdrew and agreed a thirty-year truce.

nodes.label: The second siege of Constantinople
nodes.full: Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik brought an army and an enormous fleet against the walls in the autumn of 717. A hard winter, a Bulgar attack, defecting Egyptian crews and Greek fire destroyed it; the survivors straggled home in 718.

nodes.label: Transoxiana and the Turgesh war
nodes.full: Qutayba ibn Muslim conquered the Sogdian city-states between 706 and 715, but tax demands drove repeated revolts. The Turgesh Turkish confederation nearly rolled the Arabs back to the Oxus — the 'Day of Thirst' in 724 was a rout — before Nasr ibn Sayyar stabilised the frontier in the 740s.

nodes.label: The Great Berber Revolt
nodes.full: North African Berbers, most of them Muslim but taxed and enslaved as though they were not, rose under Kharijite banners, wiping out an Umayyad army near Tangier (740) and a Syrian army at the Bagdoura (741). Umayyad authority never recovered west of Kairouan, and the revolt spilled into Spain.

nodes.label: The diwan and the garrison cities
nodes.full: Umar registered every Arab fighter and paid an annual stipend (ata) scaled by precedence in Islam, funded from the land tax of the conquered provinces. The soldiers were kept in new garrison towns — Kufa, Basra, Fustat — which became the great cities of Islam.

nodes.label: Abd al-Malik Arabises the bureaucracy
nodes.full: The tax registers, kept until now in Greek in Syria and Egypt and in Persian in Iraq, were translated into Arabic. Combined with the new coinage it made Arabic the language of the state everywhere.

nodes.label: The reformed dinar and dirham
nodes.full: After brief experiments with a 'standing caliph' image, Abd al-Malik issued a purely epigraphic gold dinar and silver dirham carrying Quranic text and no picture — the first entirely new imperial currency since Rome.

nodes.label: The fiscal problem of conversion — Umar II's rescript
nodes.full: A convert was still liable for the land tax (kharaj) on his fields, so mass conversion threatened the revenue and the state resisted it. Umar II's fiscal rescript tried to separate the land tax from the person and admit converts to the stipend — a fix that satisfied no one.
nodes.src: Gibb's "Fiscal Rescript of Umar II" study (1955)

nodes.label: The office of qadi and the beginnings of Islamic law
nodes.full: Governors appointed judges (qadis) to settle disputes among Muslims, and their rulings — drawing on the Quran, remembered practice, local custom and their own reasoning — began to harden into the 'living traditions' of each garrison city.

nodes.label: The Uthmanic recension of the Quran
nodes.full: Uthman had an authoritative consonantal text compiled and copies sent to the garrison cities, with variant collections ordered destroyed. This is the moment the Quran becomes a fixed, empire-wide book.

nodes.label: The First Fitna makes the sects
nodes.full: Out of the war over Ali's caliphate came the three enduring divisions: the Shia (the party of Ali and his house), the Kharijites (rigorists who judged sinful rulers unbelievers), and the majority who suspended judgement and became the proto-Sunnis.

nodes.label: The Dome of the Rock and the caliph as God's deputy
nodes.full: Abd al-Malik's shrine carries the earliest dated monumental Quranic inscriptions — texts affirming God's oneness and denying that God has a son, addressed pointedly at Christianity. The Marwanid caliphs styled themselves khalifat Allah, God's deputy on earth.
nodes.src: Grabar, "The Shape of the Holy" (1996); Crone & Hinds (1986)

nodes.label: The isnad and the first hadith collectors
nodes.full: As the Companions died, reports of what the Prophet said and did began to be transmitted with a named chain of authorities (isnad). Ibn Shihab al-Zuhri (d. 742) was the first to gather this material systematically.

nodes.label: Free will, sin and the community — the first theological disputes
nodes.full: Two questions split the early scholars: is a Muslim who commits a grave sin still a believer, and are human acts free or predestined (the Qadariyya insisted on free will, against a fatalism convenient to the Umayyads). These are the seeds of Islamic theology.

nodes.label: Al-Hasan al-Basri and the beginnings of renunciation
nodes.full: Preacher, jurist, traditionist and ascetic, al-Hasan al-Basri stood at the head of nearly every strand of later Islamic piety. His sermons on fear of God and detachment from the world are the earliest sustained expression of the current that would become Sufism.
nodes.src: Mourad, "Early Islam between Myth and History" (2006)

nodes.label: John of Damascus answers Islam
nodes.full: A Christian who had served in the Umayyad tax administration, John of Damascus wrote the first substantial Christian analysis of Islam, treating it as 'the heresy of the Ishmaelites' and supplying arguments Byzantine polemicists used for centuries.
nodes.src: John of Damascus, "On Heresies" ch.100; Griffith (2008)

nodes.label: The Dome of the Rock — first monument of Islamic art
nodes.full: An octagon of Byzantine construction and Sasanian and classical ornament, crowned by a golden dome — but with no human or animal figure and a band of Arabic Quranic text as its central decoration.

nodes.label: The Great Mosque of Damascus
nodes.full: Built by al-Walid I on the site of a cathedral that had been a temple of Jupiter, the Damascus mosque fixed the classic mosque form and covered its walls in a mosaic vision of paradise with no living creature in it.

nodes.label: The Umayyad desert palaces
nodes.full: Away from the mosques, the Umayyad princes built fortified pleasure-houses in the Syrian steppe with bath-suites frescoed with hunting scenes, dancing girls and the 'Six Kings of the Earth'. Umayyad secular art was figural and sensuous.

nodes.label: The aniconic turn on the coinage
nodes.full: Umayyad mints first tried a caliph in Arab dress holding a sword, then abandoned the human image entirely for pure Arabic script — a lasting boundary between Islamic sacred and secular art.

nodes.label: The early Quran manuscripts
nodes.full: The oldest Qurans — the Hijazi script leaning to the right, then the first upright Kufic — were large, sparely pointed, written for display and recitation: the founding objects of Arabic calligraphy.

nodes.label: The court poets and the first Arab art music
nodes.full: The Umayyad court kept rival panegyrists — Jarir, al-Farazdaq and the Christian al-Akhtal traded verse insults for a generation — while in the Hijaz singers like Ibn Misjah and the mukhannath Tuways set poetry to modal song, founding classical Arabic music.

nodes.label: The beginnings of Quranic exegesis
nodes.full: Explaining the Quran — its occasions of revelation, its obscure words, its legal verses — began with Companions like Ibn Abbas and grew into the discipline of tafsir. The need to make the text intelligible to non-Arab converts drove much of the early effort.

nodes.label: Arabic grammar and the two schools
nodes.full: To fix the correct reading of the Quran for a rapidly non-Arab community, scholars began to codify Arabic — its inflections, its syntax — as a formal science. Basra and Kufa developed rival methods, culminating in Sibawayh's 'Kitab'.

nodes.label: The Prophet's biography takes written form
nodes.full: Urwa ibn al-Zubayr began collecting reports of the Prophet's campaigns (maghazi); Ibn Ishaq (d. 767) assembled them into a continuous 'Life' (sira) — the framework through which the origins of Islam have been told ever since.

nodes.label: The Kharijite and Shia arguments about legitimate rule
nodes.full: Early Islam's first political theory was made by its dissidents: the Kharijites held that any pious Muslim could be imam and that an unjust ruler forfeited office and life; the Shia held that authority belonged by God's designation to the Prophet's house.

nodes.label: The first translations and the Marwanid interest in learning
nodes.full: Medical, astrological and administrative texts were turned from Greek and Persian into Arabic under the Umayyads, and the prince Khalid ibn Yazid was remembered as a patron of alchemy — the great Abbasid translation movement's Umayyad beginnings.

nodes.label: The conquest economy — booty, the fifth and the fay'
nodes.full: The first decades ran on plunder: movable spoil was divided among the fighters after the state's fifth (khums), while conquered land was mostly kept intact as fay', its taxes funding the stipend register.

nodes.label: One market from the Atlantic to the Indus
nodes.full: For the first time since antiquity a single authority held the whole land bridge between the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, and the old Roman-Persian frontier that had taxed and blocked east-west trade was gone.

nodes.label: The crop transfers begin
nodes.full: Sugar cane, rice, cotton, citrus, bananas, aubergines and hard wheat began spreading west out of India and Iran across the unified empire, along with the irrigation and crop-rotation techniques to grow them.
nodes.src: Watson, "Agricultural Innovation in the Early Islamic World" (1983)

nodes.label: Al-Hajjaj and the reclamation of lower Iraq
nodes.full: Abd al-Malik's governor al-Hajjaj drove a programme of canal-digging and marsh drainage in southern Iraq to raise land revenue, founding the garrison-and-administration city of Wasit midway between Kufa and Basra.

nodes.label: Mecca becomes a pilgrimage economy
nodes.full: Stripped of political power when the capital moved to Damascus, the Hijaz cities were rebuilt as places of pilgrimage and leisure — subsidised grain and an economy of hostels, guides and luxury trades serving pilgrims.

nodes.label: The barid — the imperial relay
nodes.full: Abd al-Malik systematised the barid, a network of post-stations with fresh mounts carrying official mail and intelligence to the caliph — the nervous system that let one court in Damascus govern from Spain to Sind.

nodes.label: Papyrus, the chancery and the 'protocol'
nodes.full: Egypt's state papyrus workshops supplied the whole empire's administration. Each roll opened with a printed header naming the caliph — first in Greek, from Abd al-Malik's time in Arabic — the origin of the word 'protocol'.

nodes.label: The Arab fleet and the Battle of the Masts
nodes.full: Muawiya, as governor of Syria, built ships and crews from the coastal population and in 655 destroyed a Byzantine fleet at the 'Battle of the Masts' off Anatolia. Command of the eastern Mediterranean was now contested.

nodes.label: Water engineering across the empire
nodes.full: The unified state maintained and extended the hydraulic works it inherited — the canal grid of Iraq, the qanats of Iran, Roman aqueducts in Syria and Spain — and moved techniques between provinces.

nodes.label: Byzantium — the enemy who lent the mosaicists
nodes.full: Umayyad-Byzantine relations were a routine of raids, tribute and prisoner exchanges, and, remarkably, cultural loans: Byzantine emperors sent craftsmen and mosaic cubes for the mosques of Damascus and Medina.

nodes.label: The eastern conquests — Sind and Transoxiana
nodes.full: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim took Sind and the lower Indus in 711; Qutayba ibn Muslim took the Sogdian cities of Transoxiana in the same years. The empire now touched India directly and bordered the Turkish steppe.

nodes.label: An inherited bureaucracy — Greek, Coptic and Persian officials
nodes.full: For two generations the empire was run by the same Greek, Coptic and Persian secretaries who had run it before, keeping the accounts in their own languages and scripts.

nodes.label: The first Arab embassy to Tang China
nodes.full: Chinese records note an envoy from the 'Dashi' (the Arabs) reaching the Tang court in 651, the year Yazdegerd III died at Merv. The two largest empires on Earth had become neighbours across Central Asia.

nodes.label: Iberia and the far west
nodes.full: Tariq ibn Ziyad's Berber-led army destroyed the Visigothic kingdom in 711 and within a decade Muslim raiders were north of the Pyrenees. The Umayyad west reached its high-water mark near Tours in 732.

nodes.label: The Sassanid Empire falls
nodes.full: The Persian Empire that had faced Rome for seven centuries collapsed in under twenty years. Its dynasty ended with Yazdegerd III's murder, but its bureaucrats, court culture and ideas of kingship were absorbed by the caliphate.
nodes.src: Pourshariati, "Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire" (2008)

nodes.label: Byzantium survives, transformed
nodes.full: Shorn of Syria, Egypt and Africa, the eastern Roman state contracted onto the Anatolian plateau, reorganised its army into land-holding regional 'themes', and became the medieval Byzantium: smaller, poorer, permanently on the defensive.

nodes.label: The limits fixed — Constantinople 718, Tours 732, Talas 751
nodes.full: Three checks a generation apart marked the edges of the first expansion: the failed siege of Constantinople in 718, the turning-back of a raid near Tours in 732, and the clash with Tang China at Talas in 751.

nodes.label: Qays and Yaman — the faction that ran the empire
nodes.full: Umayyad politics ran on a split between two blocs of Arab tribes, 'northern' Qays and 'southern' Yaman, that cut across every province and every army. The feud helped bring the dynasty down.

nodes.label: The Abbasid Revolution
nodes.full: A movement organising for decades in the name of 'the family of the Prophet' rose in Khurasan under Abu Muslim, took Kufa, and defeated the last Umayyad army at the Zab. Power passed to the Abbasid line and the mawali grievance was, for a moment, answered.

nodes.label: The mawali — Muslims of the second rank
nodes.full: A non-Arab who converted became a mawla, a client attached to an Arab tribe, expected to keep paying the taxes of a non-Muslim and excluded from the full military stipend. Islam preached equality; the Umayyad state ran on Arab privilege.

nodes.label: The women of the first generation
nodes.full: Aisha bint Abi Bakr led an army against Ali at the Battle of the Camel in 656, then spent forty years as a leading authority on hadith and law. Other women held property, ran businesses and transmitted traditions.

nodes.label: The mukhannathun and the qiyan — the makers of Arab music
nodes.full: Classical Arabic music was created in the Umayyad Hijaz largely by two groups on the social margin: the qiyan, trained singing-girls who were usually enslaved, and the mukhannathun, gender-variant men who dominated the profession.

nodes.label: The conquest slave supply and the umm walad
nodes.full: Conquest and raiding fed a huge slave trade — captives from Anatolia, the Berber lands, Central Asia and East Africa working as soldiers, farm gangs, domestics and concubines.
nodes.src: Gordon, "The Breaking of a Thousand Swords" (2001)

nodes.label: The dhimmis — the protected majority
nodes.full: For a century the empire's population was overwhelmingly Christian, Jewish and Zoroastrian, living under the 'protection' (dhimma) of the Muslim state: free to worship, liable for the poll tax (jizya).
nodes.src: Levy-Rubin, "Non-Muslims in the Early Islamic Empire" (2011)
